0. Before you start#

Part III turns the observations of Part II (activations interpolate between concepts) into one hypothesis: an activation is a sum of convex combinations of archetypes, one convex combination per active tile. Everything here is geometry of convex sets; the reminders are on the spot.

How to read this page#

Boxes marked In the paper (green-edged, “❝”) quote the paper with its page. Boxes marked “Our reading” (⚑) are our remarks, kept short; page 6 develops them with experiments. A remark box next to a proof marks a place where the paper's argument needed a correction. Proofs are in folds: read the idea box first, open the fold when you want every step. Page numbers are those of the arXiv v3 PDF.

The story in seven steps#

  1. Why a geometry. A method sees only what its assumed geometry can express (§1).
  2. The definition. Archetypes grouped in tiles; each tile is a polytope; an activation is a sum of one point per active tile (§2).
  3. Why attention gives it. A softmax head outputs a convex combination of its values; the output projection is affine; the heads are added (§3).
  4. Evidence. Straight paths leave the data, per-image archetypal analysis reconstructs well, co-activation is block-structured (§4).
  5. Implications. Concepts are points and regions; steering saturates at an archetype; the decomposition is not identifiable from one layer (§5).
  6. Limits. A working hypothesis, observational, one model (§6).
  7. Summary and exercises (§7–8).

What you need#

  • Convex hull, simplex, barycentric coordinates: hull, simplex.
  • Minkowski sum, support function, decomposability: sum, support functions, decomposability.
  • Softmax: properties. Archetypal analysis: AA.
  • The linear representation hypothesis and the observations that motivate Part III: beyond the LRH.

1. Why a geometry: what a method can see#

A dictionary method comes with an assumption about the shape of the set of activations; it can only reveal structure that this shape can express. Part II found structure that the linear shape expresses badly; Part III proposes another shape.

In the paper §7 · p. 17

“While hypotheses about representational composition are rarely stated explicitly, the geometry assumed by our methods is foundational: it constrains both their validity and the phenomena they can reveal. If sparse autoencoders implicitly answer to the Linear Representation Hypothesis, then we understand the importance of specifying the correct ambient geometry: it not only conditions how we interpret representations, but also determines the very form that our analytical methods of concept extraction can take.”

Example. A sparse autoencoder writes every activation as a=zD with few non-zero non-negative codes: the activations are assumed to lie near a union of low-dimensional cones. Whatever it finds, it reports as directions with magnitudes. If the true structure is “a point somewhere between these prototypes”, the SAE will cut it into several directions that fire together, and a reader will take that for several concepts.

The anomalies of Part II, in three lines#

  1. Atoms are neither quasi-orthogonal nor neuron-aligned (large coherence, non-flat singular values, low Hoyer score), and concept co-activation barely follows atom geometry (r=0.28).
  2. A few dense positional atoms fire on a quarter of all tokens, and position lives in a 2-D sheet that shrinks with depth: not what a sparse code predicts.
  3. Within one image tokens vary smoothly (per-image PCA maps), and local neighbourhoods stay connected after removing position: tokens look like interpolations between prototypes.

Details and numbers: page 4, beyond the LRH. The paper's proposal is that the third line is “the surface of a deeper organization”: the activation space behaves as a sum of convex hulls.

Gärdenfors' conceptual spaces, in five lines#

The cognitive scientist Peter Gärdenfors models a concept as a convex region in a space whose axes are perceptual or functional qualities (colour, weight, temperature). A point is one object. The most typical members of the region, its prototypes, are the focal, often extreme, points. Membership varies with proximity, and convexity means: if two objects belong to the category, every point on the segment between them does too. This is the picture the paper turns into a testable hypothesis (§3 below, Gärdenfors).

2. The definition#

Archetypes are grouped into tiles; each tile spans a polytope; an activation is the sum of one point per active tile, each point being a convex combination of the archetypes of its tile.

In the paper — Definition 2, Minkowski Representation Hypothesis §7 · p. 18 (App. J, Def. 3 · p. 46)

Let X⊂Rd be a layer's activation space and x∈X. Let A=(a1​,…,ac​)∈Rc×d be an overcomplete dictionary of archetypes (c≫d). We partition the archetypes into m disjoint tiles {Ti​}i=1m​, Ti​⊂{1,…,c}, and define the tile polytopes Pi​=conv(ATi​​) with ATi​​={aj​:j∈Ti​}. Then X satisfies MRH if

{(i) Minkowski sum:(ii) Block-convex coding:​X=⨁i=1m​Pi​,x=∑i∈S​zi​ATi​​,zi​∈Δ∣Ti​∣,∣S∣≪m,​

where Δk={z≥0:1⊤z=1}.

The text adds: “MRH says that a point x is a sparse composition of concept regions, with only a few tiles active ∣S∣≪m, and each active tile contributing a convex combination of its archetypes.” And: “the activation set is generated by Minkowski addition of distinct tile polytopes, with a union over attention patterns when different tiles are selected across inputs, rather than a single global linear space.”

Decoding, symbol by symbol#

A∈Rc×d
c points of Rd, stored as rows: the archetypes, the candidate vertices. They are points, not directions.
tiles Ti​
a partition of the c row indices into m groups. ATi​​ is the sub-matrix of the rows of group i. The paper's picture: one tile for position, one for depth, one for object category.
Pi​=conv(ATi​​)
everything one can reach by mixing the archetypes of tile i with non-negative weights summing to one: a polytope whose vertices are (some of) the archetypes of the tile.
(i) X=⨁i​Pi​
the set of all vectors p1​+⋯+pm​ with pi​∈Pi​: one point from every tile, added.
(ii) x=∑i∈S​zi​ATi​​
zi​ is a row vector of length ∣Ti​∣, so zi​ATi​​∈Rd is the point of Pi​ with barycentric coordinates zi​. Only the tiles in the active set S contribute.
zi​∈Δ∣Ti​∣
non-negative coordinates summing to one inside each active block. The code vector z=(z1​∣…∣zm​) has m blocks, each block is either absent or a probability vector.
∣S∣≪m
block sparsity: few tiles at a time. This is the sparsity of MRH, the counterpart of ∣suppz∣≪c in the LRH.
Reminder — Minkowski sum and simplex

A⊕B={a+b:a∈A,b∈B}. For polytopes, conv(A)⊕conv(B)=conv(A⊕B), so the vertices of the sum are among the pairwise sums of vertices. A point of Δk is a vector of weights; zAT​ is the weighted average of the archetypes. Minkowski sum, simplex and barycentric coordinates.

Worked example in the plane#

Two tiles in R2: a triangle and a segment

d=2. Tile 1 has three archetypes (0,0),(4,0),(0,2): P1​ is a triangle. Tile 2 has two archetypes (0,0),(1,2): P2​ is a segment. Both tiles are active (∣S∣=m=2).

  1. Codes: z1​=(21​,41​,41​), z2​=(41​,43​). Both are in a simplex (non-negative, sum 1).the constraint of (ii)
  2. p1​=z1​AT1​​=21​(0,0)+41​(4,0)+41​(0,2)=(1,21​).weighted average of the three archetypes
  3. p2​=z2​AT2​​=41​(0,0)+43​(1,2)=(43​,23​).same for the segment
  4. x=p1​+p2​=(47​,2).the activation is the sum of the two points
  5. All pairwise sums of vertices: (0,0),(1,2),(4,0),(5,2),(0,2),(1,4). The convex hull of these six points has only five vertices, (0,0),(4,0),(5,2),(1,4),(0,2): the sum (1,2)=(0,0)+(1,2) is interior.conv(A)⊕conv(B)=conv(A⊕B); at most 3+2=5 vertices for a triangle plus a segment
  6. The sum polygon has area 14=4+10: the triangle's area plus the segment's length 5​ times the width 10/5​ of the triangle in the direction perpendicular to the segment.sliding a segment along a polygon sweeps that extra strip
  7. Membership: (4,2)=(3,0)+(1,2) with (3,0)∈P1​ (on its bottom edge) and (1,2)∈P2​, so (4,2) is in the sum. (5,0) is not: the y-coordinate of a point of the sum is y1​+2s≥0 with p2​=s(1,2), with equality only if y1​=0 and s=0, which leaves x=p1​ on the bottom edge, x≤4.a point is in the sum iff it splits as one point of each tile
  8. Support function in direction (1,1): hP1​​=4, hP2​​=3, hP1​⊕P2​​=7.hA⊕B​=hA​+hB​; used again in §5

The paper's example: a rabbit token#

In the paper §7 · p. 18

“A token representing a rabbit might combine: (1) a convex mix from an ‘animal category’ tile (capturing rabbit-like features), (2) a convex mix from a ‘spatial position’ tile (left/center/right), and (3) a convex mix from a ‘depth’ tile (foreground/background). The final activation is the sum of these convex contributions.”

In the notation: m tiles in all, S={animal,position,depth}, zanimal​ puts most weight on a rabbit-like archetype, zposition​ is, say, (0.7,0.3,0) on (left, centre, right), zdepth​ is close to the foreground vertex. The tile “position” is the one Part II observed (a 2-D sheet, page 4); the others are the paper's guess (“it is natural to imagine one hull reflecting token position, another depth, another object or part category”). The paper does not measure these tiles.

LRH and MRH side by side#

Linear representation hypothesis (Def. 1)Minkowski representation hypothesis (Def. 2)
What a concept isa direction Di​ (unit atom)a landmark (archetype, an extremal point of a polytope) or a small constellation of landmarks whose hull is a semantic region
Constraint on the codesz≥0, ∣suppz∣≤k; no normalisationblock-wise: each active block lies in a simplex (non-negative, sums to one); few active blocks
“More of a concept”larger coefficient zi​ (unbounded)more weight on the archetype inside its tile; the weight cannot exceed 1
Shape of the set of activationsunion of low-dimensional cones/subspaces (sparse combinations of atoms)union over active sets of Minkowski sums of polytopes (the paper: convex pieces, “rather than a single global linear space”)
Steeringslide along a direction x+tDi​, with no natural stopping pointmove towards an archetype; saturates at it (§5)
Dictionary method that fits itsparse autoencoder (also k-means, NMF, PCA as special cases)archetypal analysis, the single-tile case; the paper's SAE is already archetypal (atoms in conv of the data)

Archetypal analysis is the one-tile case#

Take m=1 (or ∣S∣=1): X=P1​=conv(A) and x=zA with z∈Δc. This is archetypal analysis: every data point is a convex combination of archetypes (and archetypes are themselves convex combinations of data points, reminder). The paper uses this to test item (ii) (§4). MRH adds the sum over tiles and the block-sparse activation.

Our reading — (a) LRH is a special case of MRH: box against simplex

A bounded sparse non-negative linear code x=∑j∈S​zj​dj​, 0≤zj​≤M, is the MRH with segment tiles Tj​={0,Mdj​} (each tile has its own copy of the origin): the block of tile j is (1−zj​/M,zj​/M)∈Δ2. The two hypotheses are therefore nested, and what MRH adds is only the joint constraint inside a tile with three or more archetypes (the weights of one tile compete, they sum to one: a simplex instead of independent coordinates, which would fill a box). Developed in page 6.

Our reading — (b) item (i) and item (ii) describe different sets

The sum over all m tiles in (i) is a convex set. Item (ii) uses few tiles, so the set actually described is the union ⋃∣S∣≪m​⨁i∈S​Pi​: not convex in general (three segments [0,ej​]⊂R3 with ∣S∣≤1 give three segments, whereas the sum of the three is the cube). This is what the paper's sentence “with a union over attention patterns” says; the guide reads (i) in that sense whenever it matters. Page 6.

Our reading — (c) a criterion (iii) that the definition does not number

Definition 2 has two items, but §7.2 refers to “criterion (iii)”, “the block-sparse pattern” and “the Tiles assumption”. It is the existence of the partition into tiles with block-wise activation: the part of (ii) that says ∣S∣≪m. Read “(iii)” as “the tile structure”.

3. Theoretical account: why attention produces such a geometry#

Three arguments support the hypothesis: Gärdenfors' convex concepts, a convex-geometric tradition in earlier work, and the fact that a softmax attention head returns a convex combination of its values and that multi-head attention adds the heads' outputs. The last one is a theorem; we prove it in full.

Gärdenfors' conceptual spaces#

In the paper §7.1 · p. 18

Gärdenfors “models concepts as convex regions within domain-specific coordinate systems; points represent individual objects and prototypes correspond to focal (often extreme) points of these regions. Dimensions capture perceptual or functional qualities (e.g., color, weight, temperature), and category membership varies with proximity — if two objects belong to a category, then any point on a straight path between them remains within the category's region. From this perspective, MRH can be viewed as an operationalization of Gärdenfors' theory for decomposing visual concepts: tiles (or regions) correspond to convex concept sets, while archetypes play the role of prototypes.” The paper then asks: “is such an instantiation realistic in modern architectures, and what evidence favors regions built from points rather than purely directional features?”

convex region
a set C with x,y∈C⇒(1−t)x+ty∈C. In MRH: the tile polytope Pi​.
prototype
a focal, extreme point of the region. In MRH: an archetype (a vertex of Pi​).
quality dimensions
the coordinates (colour, weight…). In MRH a tile is a region of the whole space Rd; the paper does not say which directions play the role of quality dimensions.

What is a theory-level motivation here becomes a test later: if concepts are convex regions, then paths between two members stay inside the region. This is the idea behind the interpolation evidence of §4. The step from “a category is convex” to “activations are a Minkowski sum of polytopes” is the paper's own proposal; Gärdenfors does not make it.

Convex-geometric precedents#

In the paper §7.1 · p. 18–19 (App. J · p. 46)

Three strands, “which we organize into three strands”:

  1. (i) Piecewise-linear networks. ReLU networks partition the input space into convex polyhedral linear regions (often unbounded); work on the number of regions, depth–width trade-offs, the spline view (affine templates), the fact that trained networks realise far fewer regions than the maximum, and interpretability work that enumerates regions to extract exact piecewise-linear rules.
  2. (ii) Representation space. Convex organisation of activations and architecture-specific convex projections; population geometry (activity concentrated on low-dimensional manifolds with structured variability); concept extraction methods that constrain representations to the convex hull of a learned dictionary: k-Deep Simplex, MFAs, SpaDE (“a prototype-centric view”).
  3. (iii) Language models. Categorical and hierarchical concepts admit polytopal encodings whose geometry mirrors semantic relations (Park et al.).

None of these strands states MRH: they say that convexity and polytopes are a recurring theme. Strand (i) is about regions of the input space on which a network is affine, strand (ii) about hulls of dictionaries (the single-tile case), strand (iii) about polytopes of concepts in language models. The paper's own contribution is the sum over tiles and the link with attention.

A single head: Lemma 1 (App. Lemma 3)#

Problem. What is the set of outputs of one attention head? Answer: inside the convex hull of its values, with the attention weights as barycentric codes.

In the paper — Lemma 1 (single head) §7.1 · p. 19; App. J, Lemma 3 · p. 47

Consider one attention head with values V={v1​,…,vm​}⊂Rd and attention weights α∈Δm (α=softmax(QK⊤), outputs Y=αV). The attainable output set is Y={∑j​αj​vj​:α∈Δm}⊆conv(V). Moreover, if the pre-softmax logit map can generate any vector in Im(K⊤)+span{1}=Rm as the query varies, then Y=conv(V). In this case the outputs admit an MRH representation: codes z=α, archetypes A=V (∣S∣=1).

Reminder — softmax

softmax(x)j​=exj​/∑k​exk​. (a) Adding a constant to all logits changes nothing: softmax(x+λ1)=softmax(x). (b) It maps Rm onto the relative interior of the simplex (all weights strictly positive and summing to 1), and if α is in that interior, x=logα (entrywise) satisfies softmax(x)=α. So every strictly positive weight vector is reachable by choosing the logits, and weights equal to 0 are never reached. More.

Y
all outputs of the head when the weights range over what the head can produce.
V
the m value vectors, one per token the head attends to; m=261 for DINOv2-B with 1+4+256 tokens. They are the archetypes of this tile.
Im(K⊤)+span{1}=Rm
the reachability condition. The paper writes the image of K⊤; with the keys as the rows of K∈Rm×dk​ and a query q∈Rdk​ (column), the logit vector is Kq∈Rm, so the set is the column space of K. We use the latter; the sum with span{1} reflects the invariance (a).
Idea

Inclusion: the weights are non-negative and sum to one, so the output is a convex combination of the values. Reachability: by (b), any strictly positive weights are obtained from the logits logα; if the logits of the head can be anything (modulo a constant), any such weights, hence any point of the hull, can be produced. Boundary points of the hull are limits, not outputs.

Full proof

Step 1: Y⊆conv(V). The weights satisfy αj​≥0 and ∑j​αj​=1, so ∑j​αj​vj​ is by definition a point of conv(V).

Step 2: reachability gives the relative interior. Assume Im(K)+span{1}=Rm (column-space convention). Let α∈relint(Δm), i.e. αj​>0 for all j and ∑j​αj​=1.

  1. Put u=logα∈Rm (entrywise).well defined because every αj​>0
  2. By hypothesis u=Kq+λ1 for some query q and some λ∈R.u∈Rm=Im(K)+span{1}
  3. softmax(Kq)=softmax(Kq+λ1)=softmax(u).invariance (a)
  4. softmax(u)j​=αj​/∑k​αk​=αj​.euj​=αj​ and ∑k​αk​=1
  5. So the query q produces exactly the weights α and the output ∑j​αj​vj​.

Hence Y⊇{αV:α∈relintΔm}. Since α↦αV is linear and a linear image of the relative interior of a convex set is the relative interior of its image (Rockafellar, Thm 6.6), this set is relintconv(V). Together with Step 1 and the fact that softmax never outputs a zero weight (so Y⊆αV for strictly positive α only), Y=relintconv(V).

Step 3: the boundary. A boundary point of conv(V) (in particular a vertex vj​) would need some weight to be 0 (for a vertex, all other weights): softmax never does this, so these points are not outputs. They are limits of outputs: send some logits to −∞ (or let the temperature go to 0, Lemma 5 below). The closure of relintconv(V) is conv(V), so Y​=conv(V).

Step 4: the MRH form. The output is αV with α∈Δm: a single tile (∣S∣=1) whose archetypes are the values and whose code is α. □

Remark — what the proof of the paper needs to be exactly right
  1. Open or closed. The paper concludes Y=conv(V) (“extreme points … attained by limits of interior points”). With a finite temperature, softmax never outputs a zero weight, so the attainable set is relintconv(V) and only its closure is conv(V). This changes nothing for the geometry, but “equality” means “closure”. We say “fills the hull” below.
  2. Which space. Softmax is declared as a map Rd→Rd but used on Rm (the number of tokens), and the proof writes “y=αv” for the product αV. We read the statement as above.
  3. The condition is about the keys. The logits are Kq, an element of the column space of K (dimension at most rankK≤dk​). The condition Im(K)+span{1}=Rm needs rankK+1≥m.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: (1) move the logit sliders: the output y moves inside the blue quadrilateral and is pulled towards the value with the largest logit; (2) lower the temperature τ: y snaps to the vertex of the largest logit along the dashed green curve (Lemma 5); (3) restrict the support to S={1,2}: the output stays on the segment between v1​ and v2​, the purple sub-polytope (Lemma 6); (4) drag a value: the hull moves, the output stays in it. The smallest weight printed below is never 0 for finite τ: the output is always in the relative interior, never exactly on a vertex.

Our reading — reachability cannot hold in DINOv2-B, and the polytope changes with the image

(1) A head of DINOv2-B has dk​=64 and m=261: rankK+1≤65<261. The logits of the head span at most a 65-dimensional subspace of R261, and in self-attention the query is tied to the token, so one image realises only 261 output points. (2) The values are WV​LN(xj​), functions of the image's own tokens: the polytope is rebuilt for every image, and the argument applies to any softmax attention, trained or random. Developed in page 6.

Affine maps keep the codes: Lemma 2 (App. Lemma 4)#

Problem. Between attention and the layer's output there are linear projections and bias terms. Does the convex structure survive?

In the paper — Lemma 2 (affine transformations preserve MRH structure) §7.1 · p. 19; App. J, Lemma 4 · p. 48

If γ(x)=Wx+b is an affine transformation and x=∑j​zj​aj​ (with zj​≥0, ∑j​zj​=1), then γ(x)=∑j​zj​aj′​ with aj′​=Waj​+b: the transformed archetypes absorb the transformation and the bias, “the codes z remain unchanged”.

γ
any affine map (linear map plus bias).
aj′​
the image of archetype j; the new dictionary.
“codes unchanged”
the barycentric coordinates are the same: the relative position inside the polytope is preserved.
Full proof
  1. γ(x)=W(∑j​zj​aj​)+b.definition of γ and of x
  2. =∑j​zj​Waj​+b.linearity of W
  3. =∑j​zj​Waj​+(∑j​zj​)b.∑j​zj​=1 is what makes the bias absorbable: b=1⋅b
  4. =∑j​zj​(Waj​+b)=∑j​zj​aj′​. □the same weights, new points
Remark — several active tiles: the bias must be absorbed once

Step 3 uses ∑j​zj​=1 for one convex combination. With ∣S∣ active tiles, x=∑i∈S​zi​ATi​​ and each block sums to one, so absorbing the bias into every archetype adds b once per active tile: γ(x)=∑i∈S​zi​(WATi​​+b)−(∣S∣−1)b. The correct statement for a sum is

γ(i⨁​Pi​)=i⨁​WPi​ ⊕ {b},
i.e. absorb the bias in one tile, or add an extra one-point tile {b} (a polytope reduced to a point, with the trivial simplex Δ1={1}). In the attention block this is harmless (the output bias is a single vector), but it should not be read as “every archetype gets +b”.

Also, “LayerNorm and RMSNorm … become affine in evaluation” (App. J, p. 48): this holds for BatchNorm (frozen statistics), not for LayerNorm, whose mean and variance are computed per token at inference. DINOv2 uses LayerNorm. Page 6.

Multi-head attention: Proposition 1 (App. Proposition 3)#

Problem. A block has H heads; what is the geometry of the block output?

In the paper — Proposition 1 (multi-head attention realises MRH) §7.1 · p. 19; App. J, Prop. 3 · p. 48

Let there be H heads with value sets Vh​ (of size mh​) and per-head output projections WO(h)​. Head h produces weights αh​∈Δmh​ and output yh​=∑i​αh,i​vh(i)​∈conv(Vh​). After projection and summation

y=h=1∑H​WO(h)​yh​=h=1∑H​i∑​αh,i​WO(h)​vh(i)​∈h=1⨁H​WO(h)​(conv(Vh​)).
Every output admits an MRH representation with block-convex codes z=(α1​,…,αH​) and archetypes (WO(1)​V1​,…,WO(H)​VH​). If each head can realise any point of relint(Δmh​) up to the softmax constant, the attainable set is exactly the Minkowski sum.

WO(h)​
the part of the output projection WO​ that acts on head h (below).
WO(h)​(conv(Vh​))
the polytope of head h after projection: the tile polytope Ph​.
z=(α1​,…,αH​)
the code vector: one simplex block per head. The tiles are the heads.
Reminder — “concatenate the heads, then project” is a sum

A block concatenates the head outputs, [y1​∣…∣yH​]∈RHdv​ (each yh​∈Rdv​, dv​=64, H=12 in DINOv2-B), and multiplies by one matrix WO​∈RHdv​×d (row-vector convention). Cut WO​ into H horizontal blocks WO(h)​∈Rdv​×d. Then

[y1​∣…∣yH​]WO​=[y1​​⋯​yH​​]​WO(1)​⋮WO(H)​​​=h=1∑H​yh​WO(h)​,
because the product of a row by a stacked matrix is the sum of the products of each sub-row by its block. With the column convention of the paper this is WO(h)​yh​.

Idea

Each head gives a point of its own polytope (Lemma 1). The projection is linear, so it carries the polytope to conv(WO(h)​Vh​) (the image of a hull is the hull of the image). Adding one point from each polytope is, by definition, a point of the Minkowski sum. Conversely every point of the sum picks one point per polytope, and each of these is reached by some weights.

Full proof

Fact used. For a linear map L and a finite set V, L(convV)=conv(L(V)): L(∑j​αj​vj​)=∑j​αj​Lvj​ for the same weights, in both directions.

Inclusion.

  1. By Lemma 1, yh​∈conv(Vh​) for each head.each head is a single head
  2. WO(h)​yh​∈WO(h)​conv(Vh​)=conv(WO(h)​Vh​)=:Ph​.the fact above
  3. y=∑h​ph​ with ph​=WO(h)​yh​∈Ph​, so y∈⨁h​Ph​.definition of the Minkowski sum

Equality under reachability. Let y⋆=∑h​ph​ with ph​∈Ph​ arbitrary.

  1. There are βh​∈Δmh​ with ph​=WO(h)​∑j​βh,j​vh(j)​.definition of Ph​ as a hull
  2. If βh​∈relintΔmh​ and head h can realise any such weights, choose its query so that αh​=βh​.reachability, as in Lemma 1
  3. Then the block output is ∑h​WO(h)​yh​=∑h​ph​=y⋆.

Since the weights of softmax are strictly positive, this proves that the attainable set is the sum of the relative interiors of the tile polytopes, which is the relative interior of the sum (the relative interior of a Minkowski sum is the sum of the relative interiors); its closure is ⨁h​Ph​. MRH form. Collect z=(α1​,…,αH​) and A=(WO(1)​V1​,…,WO(H)​VH​): then y=∑h​αh​WO(h)​Vh​ with each block in a simplex. □

Remark — what the statement covers and what it does not
  • Joint reachability. The equality needs all heads to reach their weights simultaneously. Every head's queries and values come from the same tokens, so the H weight vectors are not free coordinates; the hypothesis “each head can realise any point” is stronger than “each head alone is surjective”.
  • One attention update only. A token's final representation is xL​=x0​+∑ℓ​attnℓ​+∑ℓ​mlpℓ​ followed by a final LayerNorm. The proposition describes the output of one attention sublayer: it does not cover the residual stream (a sum with all earlier terms), the MLPs (non-linear), or the final normalisation.
  • Tiles are heads, so all are active. Here ∣S∣=H for every token: every head contributes a point. The block sparsity ∣S∣≪m of Definition 2 does not appear (the “sparse” tiles of the definition would have to come from the dictionary of archetypes, not from the heads).
  • Dimensions. WO(h)​ has rank at most dv​=64, so each tile polytope has affine dimension at most 64 and the sum of 12 of them at most 12⋅64=768=d.
Our reading — what the proposition proves

Proposition 1 holds for any softmax multi-head attention, trained or not, on any input. It is a statement about the architecture, not about what DINOv2 learned: MRH needs, in addition, that the archetypes form a fixed dictionary shared across images. And in the sum the tiles are the heads, all active. Page 6.

Attention concentration: App. Lemmas 5 and 6#

Problem. Real attention is often peaked or sparse. What does the polytope picture become?

In the paper — Lemma 5 (low-temperature softmax selects vertices) App. J · p. 49

Let α=softmax(x/τ) with logits x∈Rm and temperature τ>0. Then limτ→0​∑j​αj​vj​=vj⋆​ with j⋆=argmaxj​xj​: “in the zero-temperature limit the output lies at a vertex of conv(V).” With diam(V)=maxp,q​∥vp​−vq​∥ and Δj​=xj⋆​−xj​, “the deviation from the winning vertex satisfies”

​j∑​αj​vj​−vj⋆​​≤diam(V)j=j⋆∑​e−Δj​/τ.

τ
temperature: logits are divided by τ; small τ means peaked attention.
Δj​
logit margin of the winner over j; strictly positive for all j=j⋆ if the maximum is unique.
diam(V)
largest distance between two values: the size of the polytope.
Full proof (limit and bound)

Assume the maximiser is unique, so Δj​>0 for j=j⋆. (With a tie among a set J of maximisers the limit is the barycentre ∣J∣1​∑j∈J​vj​ of the tied values, a point of a face, not a vertex.)

  1. αj​=exj​/τ/∑k​exk​/τ, and xj​=xj⋆​−Δj​, so αj​=e−Δj​/ταj⋆​ for j=j⋆.divide numerator and denominator by exj⋆​/τ, i.e. use softmax invariance
  2. αj⋆​=1+∑j=j⋆​e−Δj​/τ1​≤1.the weights sum to 1: αj⋆​(1+∑j=j⋆​e−Δj​/τ)=1
  3. As τ→0, e−Δj​/τ→0 for each Δj​>0, hence αj⋆​→1 and αj​→0: the output tends to vj⋆​.finite sum of vanishing terms
  4. Bound. ∑j​αj​vj​−vj⋆​=∑j​αj​(vj​−vj⋆​)=∑j=j⋆​αj​(vj​−vj⋆​).∑j​αj​=1 lets us subtract vj⋆​ inside; the term j=j⋆ vanishes
  5. ​∑j=j⋆​αj​(vj​−vj⋆​)​≤∑j=j⋆​αj​∥vj​−vj⋆​∥≤diam(V)∑j=j⋆​αj​.triangle inequality, then definition of the diameter
  6. ∑j=j⋆​αj​=αj⋆​∑j=j⋆​e−Δj​/τ≤∑j=j⋆​e−Δj​/τ. □step 1 and αj⋆​≤1

The sharper form is diam(V)σ/(1+σ) with σ=∑j=j⋆​e−Δj​/τ. A finite margin therefore gives an error that decays exponentially in 1/τ.

Numbers (checked)

V={(0,0),(4,0),(1,3)}, logits (1,0,−1), so Δ=(⋅,1,2) and diam=18​≈4.243. At τ=0.5: α=(0.867,0.117,0.016), y=(0.485,0.048), distance to the winner 0.487, bound 4.243(e−2+e−4)=0.652. At τ=0.25: distance 0.072, bound 0.079. At τ=0.1: 1.8⋅10−4 against 1.9⋅10−4. The bound is tight for small τ (the dominant term is α2​∥v2​−v1​∥) and holds on 20,000 random instances we tried.

In the paper — Lemma 6 (support restriction selects a sub-polytope) App. J · p. 50

Fix a subset S⊆{1,…,m} and YS​={∑j∈S​αj​vj​:α∈Δm, αj​=0 (j∈/S)}. Then YS​=conv({vj​:j∈S}). If across input regimes the support takes values in a family S of subsets, the attainable set is ⋃S∈S​conv({vj​:j∈S}), a union of lower-dimensional polytopes. When S=argmaxj​⟨w,vj​⟩ for some w, YS​ is the face of conv(V) exposed by the supporting hyperplane with normal w.

Full proof
  1. A weight vector in Δm with αj​=0 off S is the same thing as a vector of Δ∣S∣ on S. Hence YS​={∑j∈S​αj​vj​:αS​∈Δ∣S∣}=conv({vj​}j∈S​).definition of the hull
  2. Face. Let M=maxj​⟨w,vj​⟩ and S={j:⟨w,vj​⟩=M}. For y=∑j​αj​vj​∈conv(V): ⟨w,y⟩=∑j​αj​⟨w,vj​⟩≤M.weights non-negative, sum 1
  3. Equality holds iff αj​=0 whenever ⟨w,vj​⟩<M, i.e. iff α is supported on S. So {y∈conv(V):⟨w,y⟩=M}=conv({vj​}j∈S​), the face exposed by w. □strict inequality off S forces zero weight
Remark — what this lemma needs

Softmax never gives a weight exactly zero, so Lemma 6 describes sparse attention (top-k, masks, or the low-temperature limit), not the attention of DINOv2 at finite τ, whose output is always in the relative interior of the full hull. The statement “disjoint polytopes” for block-sparse attention with affinely independent values is right because barycentric coordinates are unique: the hulls of disjoint subsets of an affinely independent set do not meet.

4. Empirical evidence: Figure 17#

Three observations are offered as compatible with MRH: straight paths between tokens leave the data while graph paths do not, per-image archetypal analysis reconstructs tokens better than the 32k SAE with about ten archetypes, and the archetype co-activation matrix is block-structured. The authors call this “compatible evidence, not proof”.

In the paper — the caveat before the evidence §7.2 · p. 20

“We now provide preliminary support for each criterion. The results below should be read as compatible evidence, not proof: multiple mechanisms can mimic the same surface phenomena. Unless stated otherwise we use ImageNet-1k validation tokens from the last DINOv2-B layer; cosine distance and k-NN graphs with standard symmetrization.” And after the figure: “these observations — piece-wise linear on-manifold trajectories, efficient archetypal reconstructions, and block-structured co-activation — represent preliminary evidence rather than definitive proof. Multiple geometric hypotheses could generate similar surface patterns.” (The same text is repeated in App. J, “Limitations & Positioning”, p. 51.)

Left panel: straight chords leave the data, graph paths do not#

How to read this panel
  • What was done. Take two tokens. Path 1: the straight segment between them, cut into 100 steps. Path 2: the shortest path between them in the k-nearest-neighbour graph of the tokens (symmetrised), a polygonal line through other tokens, also resampled into 100 steps. At each step, measure the distance to the nearest token of the data set. Curves: mean with a band (dark = linear, light blue = graph).
  • Axes. x: interpolation step, 0 to 100. y: distance to the nearest sample, 0 to about 14. Both curves are 0 at the ends (the endpoints are samples).
  • Numbers. Linear: a triangle rising to about 13 at step 50 (band roughly 12–14), back to 0. Graph: rises to about 5 by step 15, plateau around 4–4.5, peaks again near 5 at steps 15 and 85. The plot's distance is Euclidean (the text says cosine, whose maximum is 2: a mismatch of the paper).
  • What MRH predicts, according to the authors. “Feasible displacements arise as sums of small face-walks within head polytopes, which are piecewise linear in barycentric coordinates yet appear curved in the ambient space.” They read the graph paths as such face-walks and conclude that the curved on-support geodesics support criterion (i).
  • What it does not show. It does not show that the straight segment leaves the support: only that its midpoint is far from every sample. The authors' own caveat applies: other geometries give the same surface pattern.
Our reading — chords leave the sample, not the support

In high dimension the midpoint of two samples is far from every sample even when the support is convex (a Gaussian, the uniform distribution on a simplex), and the graph path is within half an edge of a sample by construction. Besides, a Minkowski sum of convex sets is convex, so “straight lines leave the data” cannot support (i). What separates the tokens from a Gaussian with the same covariance is local density (the nearest neighbour is at 0.35 chord against 0.80): the tokens are clustered. The chord does leave the ellipsoid of normalised tokens, but only slightly (10% of the half-chord), ten times less than the peak of the signature, which is a sampling effect. Checked on toy data and on DINOv2 in page 6.

Middle panel: archetypal analysis against the SAE#

In the paper §7.2 · p. 20

“To test the convex coding assumption (ii), we compare Archetypal Analysis (AA) with SAE for token reconstruction. Note that AA is precisely the single-tile case of MRH (∣S∣=1), making this a direct test of our geometric assumptions. AA imposes dramatically stronger constraints: it forces all reconstructions to lie within the convex hull of observed tokens and requires archetypes to be actual data combinations. Despite these restrictive assumptions, AA matches SAE performance with remarkably few archetypes (10 archetypes per image)”; the fact that tokens are reconstructed from about 10 archetypes “indicates that embeddings concentrate on low-dimensional polytopes embedded within the ambient space”, as the probability that a random point lies in the hull of a small set of samples “decays exponentially with dimension”.

Footnote: “Archetypal Analysis seeks Z=XB where archetypes are convex combinations of data (so Z⊂conv(X)), and X≈ZA where data are convex combinations of archetypes. Both A and B have simplex constraints (columns sum to 1, non-negative).”

Reminder — decoding the footnote

In the footnote, X is the data matrix (tokens as columns), B writes each archetype as a convex combination of data points (Z=XB, so the archetypes are in the hull of the data), A writes each data point as a convex combination of archetypes (X≈ZA). Notation clash: here Z is the archetypes and A the coefficients, whereas in the main text Z is the code matrix and A the activations; and X is the data here, the image batch elsewhere. The problem is min∥X−XBA∥F2​ over simplex-constrained A,B. More on AA.

How to read this panel
  • What was done. Per image, run AA with K archetypes on its tokens and measure the mean squared reconstruction error; compare with the error of the SAE (dashed line).
  • Axes. x: number of archetypes K∈{3,5,10,20,30}. y: mean squared error.
  • Numbers. AA: 0.32 (K=3), 0.26 (5), 0.19 (10), 0.138 (20), 0.116 (30). SAE: 0.227. The curve crosses the dashed line between K=5 and K=10.
  • What MRH predicts. If activations are convex combinations of few archetypes, a convex model with few archetypes should reconstruct them well.
  • What the authors conclude. AA “matches SAE performance” with about ten archetypes per image although it is more constrained: preliminary evidence that the single-tile case captures structure.
  • What it does not show. The paper does not say how the SAE error is normalised, and the two models differ: a dictionary fitted to each image against one global dictionary of 32,000 atoms with eight active codes per token.
Our reading — AA is sandwiched between PCA and k-means

For K archetypes the per-image AA error is bounded below by that of PCA with K−1 components (the reconstructions lie in a (K−1)-dimensional affine subspace) and above by that of k-means with K clusters (the centroids are convex combinations of the data, so they are feasible). The informative question is where AA sits in this sandwich, compared with null data of the same covariance; the comparison with the global SAE is not like for like. Our errors reproduce the paper's up to ten archetypes (0.32, 0.25, 0.18 against 0.32, 0.26, 0.19) and are about 20% lower at K=20 and 30. The lemma is about optimal fits; in our runs k-means initialises AA. Page 6.

Right panel: block-structured co-activation#

How to read this panel
  • What was done. Fit archetypal analysis with about 1000 archetypes; take the coefficient matrix Z (one row per token, one column per archetype); form Z⊤Z, whose entry (i,j)=∑n​zn,i​zn,j​ is large when archetypes i and j are used by the same tokens (co-activation). Reorder archetypes by clustering. The paper does not say on which tokens the AA is fitted, nor which clustering is used.
  • Axes. Both axes: archetype index 0 to about 1000. Colour: the matrix entry (dark = 0, bright = large).
  • What to see. Bright blocks along the diagonal (from about 20 to about 150 archetypes wide, smaller towards the end), and dark between them; in particular two large dark rectangles away from the diagonal (indices up to about 650 against indices above 650, and the transpose): the first 650 archetypes and the last 350 are almost never co-activated.
  • What MRH predicts, according to the authors. Tiles imply block-structured decompositions: “even without knowledge of tile boundaries, archetypes naturally organize into co-activating groups”. They say this supports the Tiles assumption (called criterion (iii) in the text).
  • What it does not show. That the groups are simultaneously active tiles that add; the matrix also fits tokens that each use a single group (clusters).
Our reading — blocks mean clusters, not sums

A block-diagonal Z⊤Z for an AA with one simplex per token says that a token uses archetypes of one group: a union of polytopes. A Minkowski sum of simultaneously active tiles predicts the opposite: groups co-activate, with a Kronecker-like structure G1​⊗G2​ across them (the sum admits the product code αi​βj​; codes are not unique, but numerically 97% of the pairs co-activate). On DINOv2 the blocks largely follow the classes: this supports the hypothesis in its weakest form, one active group per token, and gives no sign of tiles that add up. Page 6.

5. Implications for interpretability#

If MRH holds, concepts are points and regions rather than directions, steering has a natural stopping point at an archetype, and the decomposition into tiles cannot be recovered from the activations of one layer alone.

In the paper §7.3 · p. 20

“If, and this is an assumption, the MRH holds, three immediate implications follow: (i) Concepts are no longer Directions, but Points and Regions. (ii) Steering admits a strict identifiable maximum. (iii) Decomposition is fundamentally non-identifiable.”

How to read this figure
  • Left. Two small tiles drawn in separate planes: Pi​ (green dots on a lower plate, hull shaded) and Pj​ (on the left). Their Minkowski sum is the grey 3-D block in the middle (a box whose corners are sums of one vertex of each); the arrows show the directions along which the tiles extend. It is a sketch of X=Pi​⊕Pj​; no data is plotted.
  • Right, top (pink). Directional steering: the activation (a grey blob) is moved along a straight direction (pink arrow), leaves the block, and ends far from the archetype (pink blob). The curve labelled e−∥⋅−∙∥, proximity of the steered activation to the archetype against steering strength, rises to a peak and then falls: a bell.
  • Right, bottom (purple). Archetypal steering: the activation moves towards the archetype inside the block; the same proximity curve increases monotonically with the strength (the curve is convex and reaches its maximum at the end).
  • What it does not show. The axes carry no numbers: both curves are sketches. The next subsection derives them.

(i) Concepts are points and regions#

In the paper §7.3 · p. 20

“In the context of the Archetypal representation framework, the very idea of a concept diverges from the classical linear factor picture in which semantic evidence is quantified by the magnitude of an inner product with a preferred direction. A concept is better understood as a landmark, an extremal point of the convex polytope that tessellates the latent manifold, or as a small constellation of such landmarks whose hull supports a coherent semantic region.”

Decoded: in the LRH the evidence for concept i is ⟨a,Di​⟩ (or the code zi​): a magnitude along a direction. In MRH the evidence is where the activation sits in the polytope of the tile: the barycentric weight on an archetype, or the distance to a landmark. Two activations with the same inner product with a direction can be at different places of the polytope. The nested relation of the hypotheses (box against simplex) is in §2 and page 6.

(ii) Steering has a strict maximum#

In the paper §7.3 · p. 20

“In a landmark based geometry probing no longer involves sliding indefinitely along a vector but steering an activation toward a specific point on the manifold. Once the activation reaches that landmark (or the convex cell surrounding it) the semantic signal saturates (further movement would drive the embedding off-manifold). This bounded trajectory could explain why current SAE probing gains plateau or even reverse when the scaling coefficient is pushed too far: the useful range ends at the landmark's basin of attraction. Practical probes should therefore measure how close an activation can get to the landmark set and stop once convergence is achieved, for instance by estimating barycentric weight or geodesic distance inside the convex cell rather than by extrapolating along an unbounded direction.”

Derivation of the two proximity curves. Let x be the activation, a an archetype, and take as proximity exp(−∥xt​−a∥), the quantity written in Fig. 16 (the guide uses this formula for both curves; the paper only draws them).

  1. Directional. xt​=x+tv, t≥0. ∥xt​−a∥2=∥x−a∥2+2t⟨v,x−a⟩+t2∥v∥2.expand the square
  2. This is a parabola in t with minimum at t⋆=⟨v,a−x⟩/∥v∥2 (if this is positive, i.e. if v points somewhat towards a).set the derivative 2⟨v,x−a⟩+2t∥v∥2 to zero
  3. The minimal distance is the component of a−x orthogonal to v: d⊥​=∥(a−x)−∥v∥2⟨v,a−x⟩​v∥, so the proximity first increases up to e−d⊥​ at t⋆ and then decreases, tending to 0 like e−t∥v∥: a bell. It reaches 1 only if a−x is parallel to v.distance is convex in t, so its exponential of minus is unimodal
  4. Archetypal. xt​=x+t(a−x), t∈[0,1]. Then xt​−a=(1−t)(x−a), so ∥xt​−a∥=(1−t)∥x−a∥.the point moves along the segment to a
  5. The proximity is exp(−(1−t)∥x−a∥): strictly increasing and convex in t, equal to 1 at t=1, and the path stays in the hull of any polytope containing x and a (convexity).exponential of an increasing affine function
Numbers (checked)

x=(0,0), a=(3,1), ∥a−x∥=10​≈3.162; directional steering with v=(1,0) so t⋆=3 and d⊥​=1. Proximity: directional at t=0,1,2,3,4,6: 0.042, 0.107, 0.243, 0.368, 0.243, 0.042 (the peak is e−1, symmetric about t⋆ because the distance is (3−t)2+1​). Archetypal at t=0,41​,21​,43​,1: 0.042, 0.093, 0.206, 0.454, 1. The archetypal steering reaches 1 and stops; the directional steering never exceeds 0.368 here and then decays.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: drag the start point x inside the polytope and turn the direction u (the directional step is s∥a−x∥u). When u points straight at a the orange curve peaks at 1 at s=1 and then falls; when it does not, the peak is e−d⊥​<1 and the point leaves the polytope (the readout says “OUTSIDE”). The blue curve always rises to 1 at s=1; beyond that the dashed line is the flat plateau where one stops at the landmark.

Our reading — a prediction, not a measurement

The paper runs no steering experiment here: the saturation is a consequence of the hypothesis, offered as a possible explanation for the plateaus and reversals reported for SAE steering. The curves above show that the picture follows from the definition of the two paths, not from data.

(iii) The decomposition is not identifiable#

In the paper — Proposition 2 (non-identifiability of Minkowski decomposition) §7.3 · p. 21; App. J, Prop. 4 · p. 50

Let X=⨁i=1m​Pi​ be a Minkowski sum of convex polytopes. Given only observations from X, the decomposition {P1​,…,Pm​} is generally non-unique: there exist distinct collections {Q1​,…,Qk​} such that X=⨁j=1k​Qj​. In particular, even very simple polytopes admit infinitely many decompositions as sums of line segments (zonotope generators) with varying directions and lengths.

Reminder — support function

For a non-empty closed convex C, hC​(u)=supx∈C​⟨u,x⟩: how far C extends in direction u. It is sublinear (positively homogeneous: h(λu)=λh(u), λ≥0; subadditive: h(u+u′)≤h(u)+h(u′)), it determines C (the closed convex sets are in bijection with the sublinear lower-semicontinuous functions), and it is additive on Minkowski sums: hA⊕B​=hA​+hB​ (the largest ⟨u,a+b⟩ is the sum of the largest ⟨u,a⟩ and the largest ⟨u,b⟩). More.

The paper's proof, decoded

  1. Support functions are sublinear and additive on sums, so X=⨁i​Pi​ is equivalent to hX​=∑i​hPi​​: a decomposition of one sublinear function into sublinear summands.correct: the correspondence set ↔ support function is bijective
  2. “Fix any sublinear s with 0≤s≤hX​. Then hX​=(hX​−s)+s is a valid decomposition.”this is the step that fails: it needs hX​−s to be sublinear as well
  3. Each sublinear hi​ is the support function of a unique closed convex Qi​, so hX​=∑i​hi​⟺X=⨁i​Qi​.correct, with the bijection of step 1
  4. “There are infinitely many ways to split hX​, hence infinitely many Minkowski decompositions.”only as strong as step 2
Remark — the gap in the paper's proof: hX​−s need not be sublinear

0≤s≤hX​ does not make hX​−s subadditive. Counter-example (checked numerically). X=conv{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)}, so hX​(u)=max(0,u1​,u2​). Let s=h[0,(0.2,0.2)]​, the support function of a short segment inside X: s(u)=max(0,0.2(u1​+u2​)). Then 0≤s≤hX​ (because the segment is inside X) and both are sublinear. But g=hX​−s is not: with u=(1,1), u′=(−1,0),

g(u)=1−0.4=0.6,g(u′)=0−0=0,g(u+u′)=g(0,1)=1−0.2=0.8>0.6+0.
So g is not a support function, and the triangle is not a sum “segment ⊕ something”: a triangle has no segment as a summand (Exercise 6). A random test of 105 pairs finds 15,846 violations of subadditivity. The correct condition is that s is the support function of a summand, which is far from automatic. The proposition itself is true as stated (“there exist distinct collections”), but the proof must exhibit them, as follows.

What is true: trivial and genuine non-uniqueness

Trivial non-uniqueness (always available, for any sum with a non-point summand):

  • Translate in opposite directions: P⊕Q=(P+t)⊕(Q−t) for any t.
  • Split a summand: for convex P and λ∈(0,1), P=λP⊕(1−λ)P. (⊇ by convexity; ⊆: p=λp+(1−λ)p.) Iterating gives collections of any size k>m.
  • Regroup: (P⊕Q)⊕R=P⊕(Q⊕R): the same set with a different partition into tiles.
In the paper — the rectangle example App. J · p. 50

In R2, X=[−a,a]×[−b,b]=([−a,a]e1​)⊕([−b,b]e2​). For any α∈(0,1), [−a,a]e1​=[−αa,αa]e1​⊕[−(1−α)a,(1−α)a]e1​, so X is also the sum of these two segments and [−b,b]e2​: “uncountably many distinct 3-segment decompositions”, and iterating gives k-segment decompositions for every k.

This is the second trivial case: splitting a summand into homothetic copies. The directions of the generators do not change (the paper says “varying directions and lengths”, but only the lengths vary here; the two directions are those of the sides of the rectangle).

A genuine example: the regular hexagon. Let d1​,d2​,d3​ be the unit vectors at 0∘,60∘,120∘ and T an equilateral triangle of side 1. Then

three segments[−21​,21​]d1​⊕[−21​,21​]d2​⊕[−21​,21​]d3​​​=H=T⊕(−T)(T centred at 0),
where H is the regular hexagon of side 1 (vertices (cosk60∘,sink60∘)) and the vertices of T are v0​=(−21​,−63​​), v1​=(21​,−63​​), v2​=(0,33​​).
Proof (edge vectors)

Fact: the Minkowski sum of convex polygons is the convex polygon whose edge vectors, taken in increasing order of angle, are those of the summands, merged and added when parallel (a point-reflection of a segment contributes its edge twice, once in each direction). A convex polygon is determined by its edge vectors up to translation.

  1. Each segment [−21​,21​]dk​ has edge vectors dk​ and −dk​. The three give the six unit vectors at angles 0∘,60∘,…,300∘ (since −d1​,−d2​,−d3​ are at 180∘,240∘,300∘).dk​ at 0,60,120; opposites at 180,240,300
  2. T has edge vectors e1​,e2​,e3​ of length 1 at 0∘,120∘,240∘ (e1​+e2​+e3​=0); −T has −e1​,−e2​,−e3​ at 180∘,300∘,60∘. Together: the same six unit vectors at multiples of 60∘.a triangle with exterior angles 120∘; its reflection is rotated by 180∘
  3. The two polygons have the same edge vectors, hence are translates of one another; both are centrally symmetric about 0 (a centred segment, T⊕(−T)), so they are equal. A convex polygon with six unit edges at successive 60∘ is the regular hexagon of side 1. □equal edge sequences up to translation, same centre
Segments and triangles are indecomposable (a segment is a sum of parallel segments only; a triangle only of homothetic triangles, Exercise 6), so this is a factorisation into irreducible pieces in two ways, with different numbers of factors (3 against 2): not a matter of splitting or translating. The numerical check: the vertex sets and the support functions of the two sums agree to 2⋅10−16 on 721 directions, and the area is 33​/2≈2.598 for both. More on decomposability.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: drag x in the hexagon. In “three segments” mode the green chain is t1​d1​+t2​d2​+t3​d3​; the slider s moves along the one-parameter family of decompositions of the same point (direction (1,−1,1) in the t's, because d1​−d2​+d3​=0), until a coefficient reaches ±21​ (an endpoint of its segment). Switch to “triangle + reflection”: x=p−q with p,q∈T, and slack ρ moves among the decompositions. At x=(21​,0) the segments give t=(21​,0,0) or (0,21​,−21​), and the triangles give p=21​(v0​+v1​), q=v0​: three different descriptions of one point, and the two modes disagree about which tiles carry it.

Our reading — a support cannot say which hypothesis, but a sum of segments is determined

The hexagon is also three bounded linear features in superposition (a zonotope) or two three-way categorical tiles. The support cannot distinguish them; the distribution of codes (mass on three lines through the centre, or near the six corners and the centre) can. Within the linear family the support is not ambiguous: a sum of segments does determine the directions and total lengths of its generators (only their lengths can be split), contrary to the paper's remark that the segments may vary in direction. The real ambiguity is between families of summands. In practice a dictionary is identified by sparsity and the law of the codes; that sparsity identifies tiles in general is a conjecture, not a proved result. Page 6.

In the paper — the way out §7.3 · p. 21; §8 · p. 21

“This means that, under the MRH, any method attempting to recover individual concept contributions z or concept polytopes P only from activations from a single layer alone faces a non-unique solution. However, this impossibility, at its core, also hint a possible direction. While the final Minkowski sum hide its constituent factors, the information to find the decomposition is available within previous intermediate representations. Accessing attention weights and activations from earlier layers may render the factorization tractable, and pointing interpretability efforts toward exploiting architectural structure rather than treating learned representations as opaque geometric objects.” In §8: “If MRH holds, then this very non-identifiability becomes instructive: it tells us that concept extraction cannot stop at a layer's activations. To recover meaningful structure, we must explain a layer through the sequence of transformations that formed it.”

Why this follows: the attention weights αh​ are the codes of the tiles in Proposition 1, and the values WO(h)​Vh​ the archetypes; so the head-wise split is read off the forward pass instead of being inferred from the sum. This is also why the paper's non-identifiability and its attention argument fit together: the tile structure comes from the architecture. The paper gives no experiment that uses attention weights this way.

6. Limits and conclusion#

The authors present MRH as a working hypothesis resting on observational evidence in one model, and decline to say that it contradicts the linear hypothesis.

In the paper — Limitations & Positioning App. J · p. 51

“We emphasize that the observations […] — piece-wise linear on-manifold trajectories, efficient archetypal reconstructions, and block-structured co-activation — represent preliminary evidence rather than definitive proof. Multiple geometric hypotheses could generate similar surface patterns. […] Specifically, we treat the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis (MRH) as a working hypothesis of a refinement of LRH and not a proved theory of representation. We do not claim causal identification of concepts, head ‘tiles,’ or their generative mechanisms; our evidence is observational and model-specific (DINOv2-B). Our goal is to describe robust empirical regularities (task-specific subspaces; families of depth cues; ‘Elsewhere’ patterns) and propose a geometry that makes testable predictions for future work (e.g., per-head block structure, subspace additivity across heads). We therefore refrain from stating that our results ‘contradict’ LRH; instead, we document systematic finding of regularities that go beyond a purely sparse near-orthogonal picture. All conclusions should be read as conditional on our dictionary, probes, and datasets, and we report ablations where feasible.”

“working hypothesis of a refinement of LRH”
MRH is meant to refine, not replace, the linear picture: the linear picture is kept where it works (task-specific subspaces, depth-cue families, “Elsewhere” patterns) and extended where it does not (interpolation, positional sheet).
“observational and model-specific”
no intervention (no ablation of a head, no steering experiment) and one model, DINOv2-B with registers. The head-level tiles are not identified with anything in the data.
“testable predictions”
per-head block structure and subspace additivity across heads: what a test of the Minkowski sum (as against clusters) would check.
“beyond a purely sparse near-orthogonal picture”
the claim that is supported: the LRH of Definition 1 (sparse, quasi-orthogonal) is incomplete. The stronger claim that MRH is the right replacement is not made.
In the paper — the conclusion §8 · p. 21

“Examining geometry and statistics of concepts, we found that representations depart from a strictly sparse, quasi-orthogonal regime: atoms are distributed rather than neuron-aligned, anisotropy follows task subspaces, and positional information compresses into 2D while local neighborhoods remain connected even after removing position information. These observations collectively point to an organization beyond pure linear sparsity. Synthesizing these observations, we propose the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis (MRH), in which tokens behave as convex mixtures of archetypes and activations form Minkowski sums of convex polytopes, yielding convex concept regions rather than linear directions. We explored theoretical and preliminary empirical evidence for this organisation. If MRH holds, then this very non-identifiability becomes instructive: it tells us that concept extraction cannot stop at a layer's activations. To recover meaningful structure, we must explain a layer through the sequence of transformations that formed it.”

Reading the conclusion. The chain is: observations of Part II (departure from sparse quasi-orthogonality) → hypothesis (convex mixtures, Minkowski sums) → theory (attention) and preliminary evidence → consequence (identifiability fails for a single layer, so look at the computation that built it). The last sentence is conditional (“If MRH holds”). What the paper establishes is the first arrow and the theorems of §3; what it leaves open is whether DINOv2's activations really are sums over a fixed archetype dictionary.

Our reading — where the weak points are

(1) The attention argument is a property of the architecture, and the last-layer tokens go through residual sums, MLPs and a LayerNorm that the proposition does not cover (architecture, LayerNorm). (2) The three diagnostics do not discriminate between MRH and simpler alternatives (diagnostics). (3) Non-identifiability, as stated, is too strong: the paper's proof is flawed, and what holds is that a support does not tell a linear code from a block-convex one (hexagon) (identifiability). The authors' own caveats above already say that the evidence is compatible, not probative.

7. Summary#

What to remember
  1. Definition. Archetypes A (c≫d) in m tiles Ti​; tile polytopes Pi​=conv(ATi​​); X=⨁i​Pi​; an activation is x=∑i∈S​zi​ATi​​ with each zi​ in a simplex and ∣S∣≪m. Archetypal analysis is the one-tile case. The sparse bounded linear code is the case of segment tiles at the origin.
  2. Attention. One head: αV∈conv(V), weights = codes; reachability needs rankK+1≥m and fills the relative interior. Affine maps keep the codes (bias once). Multi-head: concatenate-then-project is ∑h​yh​WO(h)​, so the output is in ⨁h​WO(h)​conv(Vh​). Low temperature: vertex, with error ≤diam(V)∑j=j⋆​e−Δj​/τ; support restriction: sub-polytope, face if S=argmax⟨w,vj​⟩.
  3. Evidence (Fig. 17). Linear chords peak at about 13 from the data, graph paths stay at 4–5; per-image AA beats the SAE (0.227) from about 10 archetypes (0.19 at 10, 0.116 at 30); Z⊤Z with about 1000 archetypes is block-diagonal. “Compatible evidence, not proof.”
  4. Implications. Concepts are landmarks and regions. Steering: directional proximity is a bell with peak e−d⊥​ at t⋆, archetypal proximity e−(1−t)∥a−x∥ increases to 1. Non-identifiability: true (trivially by translation, splitting, regrouping; genuinely for the hexagon = 3 segments = T⊕(−T)), but the paper's proof is flawed (hX​−s need not be sublinear), and a sum of segments does determine its generators' directions and total lengths.
  5. Limits. Working hypothesis, observational, DINOv2-B only, “we refrain from stating that our results contradict LRH”.

Reflexes#

  • When you see “softmax output” → barycentric coordinates of the values; strictly positive, so relative interior; low temperature → vertex.
  • When you see “affine map of a convex combination” → same weights, new points; with several blocks, the bias counts once.
  • When you see “concatenate then project” → sum of per-head projections → Minkowski sum of per-head polytopes.
  • When you see “X=⨁Pi​ and ∣S∣≪m” → ask whether it is the full sum (convex) or the union over active sets.
  • When you see “decompose a Minkowski sum” → pass to support functions; remember that a summand needs hX​−s sublinear; edges of polygons merge by direction.
  • When you see “steering saturates” → it is the distance to a landmark, e−∥xt​−a∥, not a measurement.
  • When you see “evidence for MRH” → say what else produces the same picture; the authors do.

What the next page does with it#

Page 6 takes the points flagged by the boxes above and tests them: the nesting of LRH in MRH, what the attention argument proves, LayerNorm, the three diagnostics against null data, and identifiability.

8. Exercises#

Nine exercises, from computation to proof. Every number was checked by checks/check_05.py.

Exercise 1 — A Minkowski sum by hand ★

P1​=conv{(0,0),(2,0),(0,2)}, P2​=conv{(0,0),(1,1)}. (a) List the vertices of P1​⊕P2​. (b) Is (3,2) in it? Is (2,2)? (c) Find all decompositions (2,1)=p1​+p2​ with pi​∈Pi​.

Hint

Take the hull of the six pairwise sums. For (c) write p2​=(s,s), s∈[0,1], and ask when (2,1)−p2​∈P1​.

Solution

(a) Pairwise sums: (0,0),(1,1),(2,0),(3,1),(0,2),(1,3). (1,1) is interior to the hull of the other five, so the vertices are (0,0),(2,0),(3,1),(1,3),(0,2) (five).

(b) The upper right edge is from (3,1) to (1,3), on the line x+y=4, and the sum lies in x+y≤4. (3,2) has x+y=5: no. (2,2) has x+y=4: on the edge, yes ((2,2)=(1,1)+(1,1) with (1,1)∈P1​, on its hypotenuse).

(c) p1​=(2−s,1−s) needs 2−s≥0, 1−s≥0, (2−s)+(1−s)≤2, i.e. s≤1 and s≥21​. So s∈[21​,1]: a one-parameter family, e.g. s=21​: p1​=(1.5,0.5), p2​=(0.5,0.5); s=1: p1​=(1,0), p2​=(1,1). The point has many codes: this is the non-uniqueness of codes of one decomposition, not yet of the decomposition itself.

Exercise 2 — A softmax output lies in the hull ★

V={(0,0),(4,0),(1,3)}. (a) For logits (1,0,−1) and τ=1 compute the output and check it is in conv(V). (b) Find logits for which the output is (1.4,0.6).

Hint

(b) Find the barycentric coordinates of the target first, then use logα.

Solution

(a) e1,e0,e−1=2.718,1,0.368, sum 4.086, so α=(0.665,0.245,0.090) and y=0.245(4,0)+0.090(1,3)=(1.069,0.270). It is in the hull because the weights are non-negative and sum to one.

(b) Solve α2​(4,0)+α3​(1,3)=(1.4,0.6): α3​=0.2, 4α2​=1.4−0.2=1.2, α2​=0.3, α1​=0.5. Logits logα=(−0.693,−1.204,−1.609), or after subtracting the constant log0.5, (0,−0.511,−0.916). Both give the same softmax. The weights are unique here because the three values are affinely independent.

Exercise 3 — A dimension count for reachability ★★

A head has m keys in Rdk​. (a) Show that the set of reachable logit vectors modulo 1 has dimension at most rankK, and that reachability of the whole hull needs rankK+1≥m. (b) Apply it to a head of DINOv2-B (dk​=64, m=261). (c) What does it say about the dimension of the set of reachable weight vectors?

Hint

The logit map is q↦Kq, linear.

Solution

(a) The image of q↦Kq is the column space of K, of dimension rankK≤min(m,dk​). Adding span{1} adds at most one dimension: dim(ImK+span{1})≤rankK+1. The condition of Lemma 1 asks this space to be Rm, so m≤rankK+1.

(b) rankK+1≤65<261: the condition fails by a wide margin.

(c) Softmax identifies logits that differ by a multiple of 1 and is a diffeomorphism from Rm/span{1} onto relintΔm, which has dimension m−1=260. The reachable weights form the image of a subspace of dimension at most 64 (the column space of K intersects span{1} trivially or in a line): a set of dimension at most 64 in a 260-dimensional simplex. The reachable outputs are at most a 64-parameter family, not the full hull of the values.

Exercise 4 — The affine lemma with several tiles ★★

Two active tiles give x=p1​+p2​ with p1​=(1,0), p2​=(0,1). Let γ(x)=2x+b, b=(1,1). (a) Compute γ(x). (b) Compute ∑i​pi′​ if every archetype is replaced by 2a+b (the paper's “absorb the bias in each archetype”). (c) Give the correct statement.

Solution

(a) γ(x)=2(1,1)+(1,1)=(3,3). (b) p1′​=(2,0)+(1,1)=(3,1), p2′​=(0,2)+(1,1)=(1,3), sum (4,4): too large by b=(∣S∣−1)b. (c) γ(⨁i​Pi​)=⨁i​WPi​⊕{b}: transform the archetypes by W only and add the one-point tile {b} (or add b to the archetypes of a single tile). For one tile (∣S∣=1) the paper's statement is exact because the weights sum to one.

Exercise 5 — The low-temperature bound ★★

With V={(0,0),(4,0),(1,3)} and logits (1,0,−1): (a) state the bound of Lemma 5 and compute it at τ=0.5. (b) Find a τ that guarantees an error below 0.01 and compare with the true error there. (c) Prove the bound.

Hint

Δ=(1,2) for the two losers, diam=18​. For (c) subtract vj⋆​ inside the sum.

Solution

(a) ∥y−v1​∥≤18​(e−2+e−4)=4.243×0.1537=0.652; the true error is 0.487.

(b) 18​(e−1/τ+e−2/τ)≤218​e−1/τ≤0.01 iff τ≤1/ln(218​/0.01)=0.148. At τ=0.148 the bound is 0.0049 and the true error 0.0046.

(c) y−vj⋆​=∑j=j⋆​αj​(vj​−vj⋆​) (weights sum to 1), so ∥y−vj⋆​∥≤diam∑j=j⋆​αj​ and αj​=e−Δj​/ταj⋆​≤e−Δj​/τ.

Exercise 6 — A triangle has no segment as a summand ★★★

Let T be a non-degenerate triangle in R2. Prove: (a) if T=A⊕B with A=[0,w] a segment, w=0, then a contradiction; (b) more generally, if T=A⊕B with A,B convex, then A and B are homothetic to T (or points).

Hint

Use faces: for a direction u, the face of A⊕B in direction u is the sum of the faces of A and B in direction u. For (b) use that the edge vectors of a closed convex polygon sum to 0.

Solution

(a) Let u⊥w, u=0. Then the face of A in direction u and in direction −u is the whole segment, of length ∥w∥>0. The faces of A⊕B in directions ±u are the sums FA​(±u)⊕FB​(±u), each containing a translate of A: both are segments of positive length, i.e. edges. So T would have two parallel edges with opposite outer normals u and −u. A triangle has three edges, with outer normals pairwise neither equal nor opposite (the three edge vectors sum to 0 and no two are parallel). Contradiction.

(b) The edge vectors of T are e1​,e2​,e3​, pairwise non-parallel, ∑ek​=0. The edges of a sum are the edges of the summands merged by direction, so each edge of A is λk​ek​ (a nonnegative multiple, λk​∈[0,1]) and A has no other edges. Closure of the polygon A gives ∑k​λk​ek​=0. Since e3​=−e1​−e2​ and e1​,e2​ are independent, this means (λ1​−λ3​)e1​+(λ2​−λ3​)e2​=0, so λ1​=λ2​=λ3​=λ. So A is a translate of λT (a point if λ=0), and B of (1−λ)T. The same argument gives that a segment is a sum of parallel segments only.

Exercise 7 — The two steering curves ★★

x=(0,0), a=(3,4). (a) Directional steering xt​=x+t(1,0): find t⋆, the peak proximity e−d, and say what limits it. (b) Archetypal steering: the proximity at t=0.8. (c) For which directions v does the directional curve reach 1?

Solution

(a) ∥xt​−a∥2=(3−t)2+16, minimal at t⋆=3 with distance 4 (d⊥​ = vertical offset): peak proximity e−4=0.018. No value of t does better, because a is not on the line x+t(1,0).

(b) ∥xt​−a∥=(1−t)⋅5=1 at t=0.8, proximity e−1=0.368; at t=1 it is 1.

(c) Only if a−x is a positive multiple of v, i.e. v∥(3,4) with positive sign: then d⊥​=0 and the peak is 1 at t⋆=5/∥v∥.

Exercise 8 — Decomposing a point of the hexagon ★★

Let d1​,d2​,d3​ be the unit vectors at 0∘,60∘,120∘, H=⨁k​[−21​,21​]dk​. (a) Show d1​−d2​+d3​=0. (b) Find all t∈[−21​,21​]3 with ∑k​tk​dk​=(21​,0). (c) Why does a T⊕(−T) description give yet other decompositions?

Hint

d2​=(21​,23​​), d3​=(−21​,23​​).

Solution

(a) (1,0)−(21​,23​​)+(−21​,23​​)=(0,0). (b) The second coordinate gives 23​​(t2​+t3​)=0, so t2​=−t3​; the first gives t1​+21​t2​−21​t3​=t1​+t2​=21​. With s=t3​: t=(21​+s,−s,s). The box ∣tk​∣≤21​ gives s∈[−21​,0]. Endpoints: t=(21​,0,0) and t=(0,21​,−21​); midpoint (41​,41​,−41​). A segment of solutions, because (1,−1,1) is in the kernel (a). (c) x=p−q with p,q∈T also has a family of solutions (e.g. p=21​(v0​+v1​), q=v0​), but with a different number and kind of tiles: nothing in H says which description generated it.

Exercise 9 — Sum against union, and support functions ★★

(a) In R3 let Pj​=[0,ej​], j=1,2,3. What is ⨁j​Pj​? What is the set of points with ∣S∣≤1 active tile, and with ∣S∣≤2? Is (1,1,0) in each? (b) Verify hA⊕B​=hA​+hB​ for the triangle and segment of the worked example (§2) in directions (1,−1) and (−1,−1).

Solution

(a) The sum is the cube [0,1]3 (convex). With ∣S∣≤1: the union of the three coordinate segments (an “L”-shaped star, not convex); with ∣S∣≤2: the union of the three coordinate unit squares. (1,1,0) is in the cube and in the ∣S∣≤2 set (it is e1​+e2​), not in the ∣S∣≤1 set. The set defined by (ii) with few active tiles is the union, not the convex sum of (i).

(b) Triangle (0,0),(4,0),(0,2), segment (0,0)–(1,2), sum with vertices (0,0),(4,0),(5,2),(1,4),(0,2). Direction (1,−1): hT​=max(0,4,−2)=4, hS​=max(0,−1)=0, hT⊕S​=max(0,4,3,−3,−2)=4=4+0. Direction (−1,−1): hT​=max(0,−4,−2)=0, hS​=max(0,−3)=0, hT⊕S​=max(0,−4,−7,−5,−2)=0.
